summary: Scale AI benchmark of 284 expert-written, deliberately under-specified, single-turn tasks over 18 copyleft repositories (Go 106, Python 84, TS/JS 56, C/C++ 38; no Java). It has three workflows. Codebase Q&A (124 tasks: architecture, root cause, onboarding, security, API usage) requires runtime evidence. Test Writing (90 tasks) is graded by mutation kill plus rubric. Refactoring (70 tasks) is graded by regression tests plus rubric. Models run three trials in their native CLIs (Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI) and in bash-only mini-SWE-agent. Best overall Pass@1 is about 42-43% (GPT-5.4/Codex, Opus 4.7/Claude Code), Q&A tops out at about 41%, and the strongest open-weight model (GLM 5) scores 24%. Rubrics are judged by Opus 4.5, validated against human grades.

claims.claim: GPT-5.4 (Codex) and Opus 4.7 (Claude Code) lead at 43.49±3.32 and 41.89±3.31 Pass@1; the best open-weight model GLM 5 scores 24.03
claims.evidence: Table 1: three trials per model-task, Wilson 95% CIs at trial level; Q&A Pass@1 40.8 and 40.3 respectively. The two leaders' CIs overlap, so 'lead' is a tie.

claims.claim: Top models rely on extensive codebase exploration and runtime-driven reasoning
claims.evidence: Fig. 3(a) plots Pass@1 against mean code executions and answer length for 8 models on mini-SWE-agent; manual trajectory inspection describes servers started and live requests sent. This is a between-model association (stronger models also execute more), with no intervention that removes execution. Failure classification of 'No Runtime Evidence' (46% of Claude Q&A failures) is done by an LLM (Opus 4.6) without validation.

claims.claim: Engineering quality lags functional correctness: refactors would pass at 60-80% on tests alone, and rubric pass rates are 15-40 points lower (10-15 points for test writing)
claims.evidence: Fig. 2 across 8 models on a common scaffold, with worked examples (a no-op mutation surviving GPT-5.4's tests; Sonnet 4.6 leaving dead state in a k6 refactor). The rubric axis depends on the LLM judge.

claims.claim: Consistency is poor: Pass3 (all three trials pass) is 30-50% below Pass@1 for the best configurations
claims.evidence: Table 1 (e.g., 29.2 Pass3 vs 43.49 Pass@1 for GPT-5.4) and App. E Fig. 12, from logged trials.

claims.claim: Native vendor scaffolds outperform the minimal bash-only scaffold for the same model
claims.evidence: Table 1: Opus 4.7 41.9 native vs 38.9 mini-SWE-agent; native scaffolds make 1.5-2x more tool calls (App. C, Fig. 7). The native gain bundles subagents, planning/TODO tools and vendor prompts, which are not separated.

App. H. Three-judge pairwise κ is 0.74-0.84 over 1,306 rubric judgments. Opus 4.5 self-consistency κ is 0.983 over 510 judgments from 5 repeats. Human agreement over 200 rubric items is κ 0.78/0.84/0.88 for Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5 and Opus 4.5, so the highest-agreeing Opus 4.5 was chosen. The human sample covers responses from Opus 4.5 and GPT-5, not the headline models.

patterns.note: This is the most direct measurement in the KB of agents answering developer onboarding, architecture and root-cause questions about real repositories. The best systems pass about 41% of Q&A tasks (GPT-5.4 47% on the Onboarding sub-category, Gemini 3.1 Pro 12-21%), and only about 29% of all tasks pass consistently across three trials. Agents are not compared with docs, static-only reading, or human onboarding, so this shows capability limits rather than whether QA agents beat an alternative.

Q&A tasks frame deep comprehension as the step that 'precedes any code change', and trajectories show explore-then-execute behaviour. The link to success is a between-model correlation (Fig. 3a), not a comparison of discovery strategies.
Prompts are deliberately under-specified, but tasks are single-turn and the agent cannot ask; clarification is explicitly deferred to future work (§6). No evidence on clarifying questions.

On Q&A, Claude Code spawns subagents in 96-99% of trials (Opus 4.6 averages 2.6), while Gemini CLI uses them in about 1% despite having the tool. The native-scaffold gain over mini-SWE-agent is not decomposed, so subagent contribution is not isolated.

A rubric-based LLM judge on atomic YES/NO criteria is validated against human graders (κ 0.88 for the chosen Opus 4.5 judge, versus 0.78-0.84 for alternatives), is near-deterministic across repeats (κ 0.98), and agrees with other judge families (κ 0.74-0.84). Caveats: 200 human items, graded on Opus 4.5 and GPT-5 outputs, and an Anthropic judge scoring Claude models without a same-family bias check.

Execution-based checks alone (regression tests for refactors) would pass 60-80% of submissions that rubric review rejects as half-done; mutation testing is a stronger execution check that catches assertion-free or trivially true tests. Test execution is necessary but overstates quality when used alone.
All models perform poorly on the Acceptance Tests sub-category of Test Writing relative to unit and integration tests (App. F, Fig. 13); no numbers are discussed in the body and nothing is compared.
New benchmark covering Q&A, test writing and refactoring, with combined programmatic and rubric grading and released tasks.
Reports cost per task (about $0.35 for Gemini 3 Flash up to about $1.90 for GPT-5.4 on Q&A plus Test Writing); Opus 4.6/4.7 are cost-dominated by GPT-5.4. Descriptive only.

methodology.sample: 284 tasks (124 Q&A, 90 Test Writing, 70 Refactoring) over 18 copyleft repositories; 3 trials per model-task
methodology.baselines: Cross-model; native vendor scaffold vs mini-SWE-agent for the same model; no human or documentation baseline
methodology.models: GPT-5.4, GPT-5.3 Codex, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, GLM 5 and other open-weight models; Opus 4.5 judge
methodology.variance: Three trials; Wilson 95% CIs at the trial level; Pass@3, Pass@1 and Pass3 reported
methodology.ablations: Scaffold comparison only; no execution, subagent or tool ablation
methodology.contamination_controls: Copyleft repositories, expert-rewritten problem statements, a gold-patch similarity memorization screen (Jaccard 0.35-0.51), and a search for solution lookups (4 of 210 trials, all failed); internet access was enabled
methodology.languages: Go, Python, TypeScript/JavaScript, C/C++; no Java or JVM

standards.artifacts: Tasks and evaluation released at github.com/scaleapi/SWE-Atlas; runs via the Harbor framework

biases.detail: Opus 4.5 grades rubrics for Opus 4.6/4.7 and Sonnet 4.6. Human validation covered Opus 4.5 and GPT-5 outputs, and no self-preference test was run.
Refactoring gold patches exist in public git history and agents had internet access; mitigated by a similarity screen and a lookup audit, as the authors acknowledge.
No Java or Kotlin repositories; language results vary widely (C/C++ about 17-24% vs Python/TS about 45-51%).
The failure-mode classification in Fig. 3(b), including the 46% 'no runtime evidence' figure, is produced by Opus 4.6 without human validation.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and open-weight labs; no Scale model
coi.detail: Scale sells data and evaluation services to the labs whose models are ranked, which creates a mild interest in a benchmark that differentiates frontier models, but no own product is evaluated, and tasks and graders are released.

verdict_reason: A careful benchmark with three trials and CIs, a human-validated rubric judge, contamination checks and released tasks. Its Codebase Q&A track directly measures onboarding and comprehension questions. Its causal language about exploration and runtime reasoning is correlational, and it lacks Java coverage and multi-turn clarification, which limits transfer.
applicability: This is the best current evidence for the onboarding and Q&A part of the harness, and it argues for treating agent answers as drafts. Even the best agents pass about 40% of expert onboarding and architecture questions and are inconsistent across reruns. Before an agent's explanation of a Spring Boot service or ingestion flow is shown to a new developer as fact, or captured into the knowledge base, the harness should (1) require citations to files and symbols plus runtime evidence (a request actually sent against a local profile, a log line, a test run); (2) rerun the question and flag answers that disagree between runs; and (3) route it through human review before capture. Supply each repository with a runnable local profile and fixtures so agents can gather runtime evidence, which top models exploit. Treat 'tests pass' as insufficient for agent-written tests and refactors, and add mutation testing (PIT for Java) plus a rubric review. Caveats: no Java, single repositories rather than the team's 4+ repo setting, and no multi-turn clarification.

conflicts_with.detail: ProgramBench finds a 9-judge LLM panel only moderately consistent (pooled Fleiss κ 0.57) at classifying cheating trajectories, while SWE Atlas reports substantial judge agreement (κ 0.74-0.88 with humans and across families). Likely reconcilable: atomic YES/NO rubric items versus an ambiguous policy boundary.
